name: Kingdom of Croatia (1102-1526)
info: The Kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia in union with Hungary from Coloman's coronation at Biograd in 1102 until Louis II's death at Mohács in 1526, keeping its own Sabor, ban and nobility.

facts.capital: Biograd (coronation of 1102); the bans ruled from various seats, and Knin and Zagreb were leading towns
facts.founder: Coloman of Hungary, crowned King of Croatia and Dalmatia in 1102
facts.predecessor: Kingdom of Croatia under the Trpimirović and Svetoslavić dynasties
facts.successor: Habsburg monarchy (Ferdinand I elected at Cetin in 1527)

t: Coloman of Hungary was crowned King of Croatia and Dalmatia at Biograd in 1102, and the union with Hungary lasted, in changing forms, until 1918.
Croatia kept institutions of its own within the union: the Sabor, an assembly of nobles, the ban as the king's governor, and a customary law distinct from Hungary's.
The Ottoman wars of the 15th and 16th centuries, from the defeat at Krbava Field in 1493 to Mohács in 1526, reduced Croatia's territory and left it weak and divided.
dyk: The Pacta Conventa, the supposed agreement between Coloman and twelve Croatian noble tribes, survives only in a 14th-century transcript, and most modern Croatian historians regard it as a forgery.
ev: Coloman defeats King Petar's troops at the Battle of Gvozd Mountain
Coloman is crowned King of Croatia and Dalmatia in Biograd
The Mongols sack Zagreb and Čazma; Béla IV makes Gradec a free royal city
Paul I Šubić of Bribir, ban from 1274 and hereditary ban from the 1290s, rules most of Croatia as a practically independent ruler
Venice signs the Treaty of Zadar, giving up Dalmatia to Louis I
Ladislaus of Naples sells his rights in Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats
The Croatian army is defeated by the Ottomans in the Battle of Krbava Field
Louis II dies at the Battle of Mohács

sections.foundation:
Demetrius Zvonimir, of the Svetoslavić branch of the House of Trpimirović, had married Helen of Hungary, sister of King Ladislaus I. After Zvonimir died in 1089 and his successor Stephen II died without an heir in 1091, civil war broke out. Nobles around Helen offered the throne to Ladislaus I, who conquered Slavonia in 1091 but was halted near Mount Gvozd and forced to withdraw by a Cuman attack on Hungary.

His nephew Coloman continued the campaign and in 1097 defeated King Petar, who was killed in the Battle of Gvozd Mountain. Negotiations followed with the Croatian lords, and in 1102 Coloman was crowned in Biograd. The Pacta Conventa describes twelve noble tribes recognising him in return for keeping their lands and tax exemption; it is not an authentic document of 1102, but some agreement almost certainly existed. Historians long disputed whether the union was a personal union or an annexation; Hungarian legal historians today see it as most like a personal union.
sections.socioeconomy:
In the 12th century a layer of powerful noble families formed, mostly descendants of the original twelve noble tribes. They held whole counties and presided over local courts, so the local population was entirely separated from any state organisation. The leading families were the Šubić of Bribir, the Babonić in western Slavonia, the Kačić of Omiš, known for piracy, and the Frankopan, Princes of Krk. After the Second Crusade the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller gained property in Croatia.

Kings sought to balance the nobles by making towns free royal cities: Varaždin in 1220, Vukovar in 1231, Virovitica in 1234, Gradec in 1242, Križevci in 1252 and others. Free cities elected their own councils and courts, collected their own taxes and managed their own trade. After the Treaty of Zadar of 1358 the economy flourished, especially in the coastal cities, new royal towns grew on trade routes, and richer merchants came to dominate the towns.
sections.military:
Hungarians and Croats fought Venice and Byzantium for the Dalmatian coastal cities. In 1116 Venice defeated Ban Cledin and seized Biograd, Split, Trogir, Šibenik and Zadar; the cities changed hands repeatedly, and in 1202 Venice and the Fourth Crusade sacked Zadar. In 1242 the Mongols plundered Slavonia, sacked Zagreb and attacked Klis, where they failed to take the fortress; afterwards fortresses such as Medvedgrad were built and nobles were allowed to build castles.

After 1463 the Ottomans raided Croatia regularly. Count Petar Zrinski won the first major victory near Glina in 1478, and in 1483 Ban Matthias Geréb and the Frankopans defeated about 7,000 akıncı at the Una River. On 9 September 1493 a Croatian army of about 10,000 suffered a huge defeat at Krbava Field. Ban Petar Berislavić won at Dubica in 1513 but was killed in 1520, Knin fell on 29 May 1522, and Petar Kružić defended Klis for almost 25 years.
sections.governance:
Croatia was ruled for the king by a governor, the ban. From 1198 Croatia and Slavonia were held by Dukes of Croatia, who ran their duchy as semi-independent rulers with a ban beneath them. In 1225 the territory was divided between a Ban of Croatia and Dalmatia and a Ban of Slavonia; the offices were often held by one person after 1345 and merged by 1476. The country was divided into counties (županije) under counts who were local hereditary nobles ruling by Croatian customary law. The Sabor, an assembly of nobles, and the ban preserved institutions of separate statehood.

Croatian custom, the consuetudo Croatorum, differed from Hungarian law; in 1361 Louis I ordered Ban Nicholas Szécsi to judge by Hungarian custom instead. In Church affairs, Croatia south of Gvozd was under the Archbishop of Split, and Slavonia under the Archbishop of Kalocsa.
sections.impact:
The kingdom's legal and noble institutions, and the continuous mention of the Kingdom of Croatia and of Croats in official documents, preserved a separate pre-modern Croatian nation within the union with Hungary. Its customary law was later kept by Venice in Dalmatia and codified in statutes such as those of Vinodol and Poljica.

Powerful nobles at times ruled almost alone: Paul I Šubić of Bribir, ban from 1274, became hereditary ban in the succession war of the 1290s, took Bosnia in 1299, issued his own money and helped bring Charles I of Anjou to the throne. In 1519 Pope Leo X called Croatia the forefront of Christianity (Antemurale Christianitatis) for its soldiers' part in the wars with the Ottomans. Three crowned lion heads represented the kingdom from the 13th century, and the checkerboard became the official arms after 1527.
sections.decline:
Royal authority was repeatedly undermined by the nobles. After Paul Šubić's death in 1312 his family declined, and Ivan Nelipić ruled from Knin outside the king's authority until 1344. The anti-court movement after 1382 brought the capture of Queen Mary and her mother Elizabeth, Elizabeth's murder in 1387 and the Bloody Sabor of Križevci in 1397. In 1409 Ladislaus of Naples sold his rights in Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats.

The Ottoman advance after the fall of Bosnia in 1463 reduced Croatia's territory and left it weak and divided. On 29 August 1526 the Hungarian army was routed at Mohács and Louis II was killed. With two rival kings elected in Hungary, the Croatian Sabor unanimously elected Ferdinand of the House of Habsburg as King of Croatia at Cetin on 1 January 1527, while the Slavonian nobility sided with John Zápolya. Both crowns passed to the Habsburgs and the realms became part of the Habsburg monarchy.

summary: From 1102 to 1526 the Kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia shared its king with Hungary while keeping its own ban, Sabor, counties and customary law. Its history was one of struggle with Venice for Dalmatia, powerful noble houses such as the Šubić, the Mongol invasion and the Ottoman wars, ending with Mohács and the Habsburg election at Cetin.
references: John Van Antwerp Fine, The Early Medieval Balkans: A Critical Survey from the Sixth to the Late Twelfth Century (1991)
John Van Antwerp Fine, The Late Medieval Balkans: A Critical Survey from the Late Twelfth Century to the Ottoman Conquest (1994)
Frederick Bernard Singleton, A short history of the Yugoslav peoples (Cambridge University Press, 1985)
Glenn E. Curtis, A Country Study: Yugoslavia (Former) (Library of Congress, 1992)

pointDescs.1102: Coloman is crowned King of Croatia and Dalmatia in Biograd, joining the crown to Hungary's.
pointDescs.1116: After Coloman's death Venice defeats Ban Cledin and seizes Biograd, Split, Trogir, Šibenik and Zadar.
pointDescs.1133: Béla II wins back the lost Dalmatian cities except Zadar.
pointDescs.1167: The Byzantines conquer Croatia south of the Krka and Bosnia, holding them until 1180.
pointDescs.1180: On Manuel I Komnenos's death the Byzantine Empire gives up the lands it had taken.
pointDescs.1242: The Mongols sack Zagreb and Čazma and leave the land devastated and in famine.
pointDescs.1312: Paul I Šubić of Bribir dies after ruling from Gvozd to the Neretva as a practically independent ban.
pointDescs.1327: Amid conflicts between Ivan Nelipić and the Šubići, Venice takes Split.
pointDescs.1358: The Treaty of Zadar gives Louis I all of Dalmatia; Croatia is united under one administration and its economy flourishes.
pointDescs.1387: During the anti-court movement Elizabeth is strangled at Novigrad and Sigismund is crowned.
pointDescs.1409: Ladislaus of Naples sells his rights in Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats.
pointDescs.1463: The fall of the Kingdom of Bosnia opens Croatia to regular Ottoman raids.
pointDescs.1493: The Croatian army is heavily defeated at the Battle of Krbava Field.
pointDescs.1522: Ottoman forces under Gazi Husrev-beg capture Knin on 29 May.
pointDescs.1526: Louis II dies at the Battle of Mohács and the crown passes to the Habsburgs.
